title: Europe: Farmhouse & Folk Ferments Beyond the Style Books
attribution: Beyond the well-catalogued beer and wine traditions, Europe keeps a set of farmhouse and folk ferments — juniper-filtered Finnish sahti, Slavic bread kvass, honey medovukha — some now protected (sahti holds an EU TSG). Documented from producer and ethnographic sources; values are typical.

styles.name: Sahti (EU TSG)
styles.impression: Finland's ancient farmhouse ale — hazy, dense, banana-and-clove from farmhouse yeast, and unmistakably resinous from being filtered through juniper.
styles.comments: Holds an EU Traditional Speciality Guaranteed registration. Uncarbonated, cloudy, and drunk fresh — it does not keep. Rye and juniper define it more than hops.
styles.ingredients: Barley (and often rye) malt, mashed and lautered through a trough (kuurna) lined with juniper twigs and berries; hops minimal or absent; fermented with baker's or farmhouse yeast, usually unboiled.

styles.name: Gotlandsdricke / Koduõlu (Baltic Farmhouse Ale)
styles.impression: The wider Nordic-Baltic farmhouse ale family — smoky, juniper-infused, rye-inflected country beers kept alive by home brewers.
styles.comments: Gotlandsdricke (Sweden), koduõlu (Estonia), maltøl (Norway). The Norwegian branch preserved the kveik yeasts now prized worldwide.
styles.ingredients: Barley and rye malt, often smoke-dried; juniper infusion; indigenous 'kveik'-type farmhouse yeasts.
styles.tags: nordic, baltic, farmhouse, kveik, juniper, traditional

styles.name: Kvass (квас)
styles.impression: Slavic fermented rye-bread drink — dark, tangy, bready and barely alcoholic, drunk as a summer refresher and the base of cold soups.
styles.comments: Ubiquitous across Russia, Ukraine and Eastern Europe. Usually treated as a soft drink; the alcohol is incidental. Base of okroshka soup.
styles.ingredients: Stale rye (or barley) bread, water, sugar and often mint or raisins, fermented briefly by wild yeast and lactic bacteria.

styles.name: Medovukha & Lithuanian Midus (Honey)
styles.impression: Slavic and Baltic honey ferments — the folk ancestors of mead, often spiced and historically boiled, ranging from light and quaffable to rich and strong.
styles.comments: Medovukha (Russia), midus (Lithuania, protected traditional recipes). Distinct in method from Western show mead — faster, spiced, sometimes hopped.
styles.ingredients: Honey and water, frequently with hops, spices or berries; medovukha was traditionally a quicker, sometimes-boiled brew than aged mead.
styles.tags: slavic, baltic, honey, medovukha, midus, traditional
